kunyah: Abu Hurayrah — reports differ on his given name; most say Abd ar-Rahman ibn Sakhr
teaser: He fainted from hunger in the mosque and people stepped over him thinking he was mad.

layers.title: Who
layers.subtitle: A Yemeni with no property and no clan
layers.content:
He came out of Daws, a clan of Azd in the Yemen, and the sources cannot agree on what his mother named him. Most say Abd ar-Rahman ibn Sakhr. Reports differ so widely that the safest thing to say about the most quoted man in Islamic history is that nobody is certain of his name.

The kunyah stuck instead. Abu Hurayrah — father of the kitten. He used to carry a small cat about with him, and the name people gave him for that is the name the whole ummah has used ever since.

When he reached Madinah he had nothing. No trade, no land, no clan in the city to fall back on. He joined the men of the Suffah, the shaded verandah at the edge of the Prophet's ﷺ mosque where the destitute slept.

He described those years himself, without softening them. He used to collapse between the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the door of Aisha's room, and passers-by would put a foot on his neck, certain he was possessed or having a fit. He was not. He was hungry.

He was also, by his own account, the man in Madinah with the least to do and the most attention to spare.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of ar-Riqaq — Abu Hurayrah on collapsing from hunger between the pulpit and Aisha's chamber
layers.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of ar-Riqaq and Book of Knowledge; the verandah of the Suffah is described in the glossary to Aisha Bewley's translation of Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, as a shelter attached to the Prophet's ﷺ Mosque where the poor lodged

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: A tribe prayed for, a mother who refused
layers.content:
Islam reached Daws through one of their own. At-Tufayl ibn Amr ad-Dawsi became Muslim while the Prophet ﷺ was still in Makkah, went home to call his people, and got nowhere for years. He came back worn down and asked the Prophet ﷺ to invoke Allah against Daws. The Prophet ﷺ invoked Allah to guide Daws instead.

They came. In early 7 AH at-Tufayl arrived with seventy or eighty households of his people, and the Prophet ﷺ was away at Khaybar, so they went on to Khaybar to reach him. Abu Hurayrah came in with that migration.

What it cost him was his mother. She stayed on the religion of her people, and when he pressed her she said things about the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he could not repeat. He went to the Prophet ﷺ in tears and asked him to pray that she be guided. The Prophet ﷺ prayed. Abu Hurayrah went back to the house and found her behind the door, washing, and she said the shahadah to him through it.

He ran back to the mosque weeping again, this time for the other reason.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih Muslim, Book of the Virtues of the Companions, narrated by Abu Hurayrah — the du'a for his mother
layers.source: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the Delegation of Daws, early 7 AH, at-Tufayl ibn Amr and the du'a for their guidance; Sahih Muslim, Book of the Virtues of the Companions, for the du'a for his mother

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: Four years, and not one of them wasted
layers.content:
He arrived in the seventh year and the Prophet ﷺ died in the eleventh. Everything Abu Hurayrah carried, he collected inside that window.

He was frank about the method. He complained one day that he heard a great deal from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and then forgot it. He was told to spread out his cloak. The Prophet ﷺ made a gathering motion with his hands into it and told him to draw it to his chest. Abu Hurayrah said he never forgot anything after that.

He also asked questions the others did not think to ask. He once asked who would be the most fortunate person to receive the Prophet's ﷺ intercession on the Day of Rising. The Prophet ﷺ answered that he had expected Abu Hurayrah to be the first to ask, because he had seen his appetite for hadith. Then he told him: the one most fortunate with my intercession is whoever says there is no god but Allah, sincerely, from his heart.

And he kept a careful account of who was ahead of him. No Companion, he said, narrated more from the Prophet ﷺ than he did — except Abdullah ibn Amr, who used to write, and he did not write.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Knowledge — the spread cloak, the question about intercession, and Abu Hurayrah's statement about Abdullah ibn Amr writing
layers.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Knowledge and Book of ar-Riqaq, narrated by Abu Hurayrah

layers.title: The Trial
layers.subtitle: Accused of talking too much, he recited an ayah
layers.content:
The complaint against him began in his own lifetime and has never entirely stopped. People said Abu Hurayrah narrates a great deal. Some of them meant it as a question about his honesty.

He gave two answers, and both are recorded.

The first was an ayah. Were it not for two verses in the Book of Allah, he said, he would not have narrated a single hadith — and he recited «إِنَّ الَّذِينَ يَكْتُمُونَ مَا أَنزَلْنَا مِنَ الْبَيِّنَاتِ وَالْهُدَى» — those who conceal what We have sent down of clear proofs and guidance. He was not narrating because he enjoyed it. He was narrating because silence had a verse against it.

The second answer was his poverty, turned around. The Muhajirun, he said, were occupied with their trade, and the Ansar were occupied with their land. He was a poor man who stayed close to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on an empty stomach. He was present when they were absent, and he remembered when they forgot.

That is the whole argument, and it is a strange one. The thing that put his face on the floor of the mosque is the thing that made him the memory of the ummah.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Knowledge, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
layers.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Knowledge — Abu Hurayrah citing Surah al-Baqarah 2:159, and his statement about the Muhajirun's trade and the Ansar's land

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: Two vessels, and one he never poured out
layers.content:
He taught in Madinah for the rest of his life, and the number of men who sat and took from him runs into the hundreds. Follow almost any chain of hadith backwards and you will meet him.

He lived into the years when the ummah turned on itself, and he did not add his voice to the quarrel. What he said about that period was that he was carrying two vessels of knowledge. One he had poured out. If he poured out the other — what he had been told about the trials that were coming — the people would have stoned him for it. So he kept it. A man with a reputation for saying everything, deliberately not saying something.

Reports differ on the year of his death; 57, 58 and 59 AH are all given. He was buried at al-Baqi'.

What the ummah kept from him is not only the hadith. It is the habit that produced them: sit closer than is comfortable, ask the question you are embarrassed to ask, and assume you will forget unless you do something about it today.

And the answer to his own best question is still available to anyone. Say it sincerely, from the heart.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Knowledge and Book of the Trials, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
layers.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Knowledge and Book of the Trials (Kitab al-Fitan), narrated by Abu Hurayrah; reports differ on the year of his death

quiz.prompt: Where did Abu Hurayrah say he used to collapse, and why did people step over him?

options.text: At the gate of Khaybar, because of a wound
Between the Prophet's ﷺ pulpit and Aisha's chamber, and they thought he was mad — he was hungry
On the road from Yemen, from exhaustion
In the market of Madinah, from grief at his mother's death

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of ar-Riqaq, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
quiz.scholar_reflection: He told this about himself. The most quoted man in the ummah's history preserved the detail that strangers used to put a foot on his neck.

quiz.prompt: At-Tufayl ibn Amr came back from Daws exhausted and asked the Prophet ﷺ to invoke Allah against them. What did the Prophet ﷺ do?

options.text: He invoked Allah against Daws, and they were struck by drought
He told at-Tufayl to leave them and stay in Madinah
He invoked Allah to guide Daws instead
He sent a second teacher to them

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the Delegation of Daws
quiz.scholar_reflection: Seventy or eighty households of Daws reached him at Khaybar in early 7 AH. Abu Hurayrah was among them. The du'a that was not made mattered as much as the one that was.

quiz.prompt: Which two verses did Abu Hurayrah recite when people accused him of narrating too much?

options.text: The verses on concealing what Allah has sent down of clear proofs and guidance
The verses on the hypocrites of Madinah
The Throne Verse
The verses on the spoils of Khaybar

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Knowledge — Abu Hurayrah citing Surah al-Baqarah 2:159
quiz.scholar_reflection: He said that without those two verses he would not have narrated one hadith. He was not defending a hobby. He was pleading an obligation.

quiz.prompt: Which Companion did Abu Hurayrah name as having narrated more than him, and for what reason?

options.text: Ibn Abbas, because he was the interpreter of the Qur'an
Anas ibn Malik, because he served ten years
Abdullah ibn Amr, because he used to write and Abu Hurayrah did not
Ibn Umar, because he followed the Sunnah most exactly

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Knowledge, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
quiz.scholar_reflection: One man's memory against another man's ink, and the man with the memory conceded the point without complaint.

quiz.prompt: How did Abu Hurayrah explain being present for so much more of the Prophet's ﷺ speech than other Companions?

options.text: He was appointed as the Prophet's ﷺ scribe
The Muhajirun were busy with trade and the Ansar with their land; he was poor and stayed close
He lived inside the Prophet's ﷺ household
He was given a special seat in the mosque

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Knowledge, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was present when they were absent, and remembered when they forgot. He said it plainly, as a matter of arithmetic rather than merit.

quiz.prompt: Abu Hurayrah asked the Prophet ﷺ the question nobody else asked, and was told his eagerness for hadith had been noticed. What stops you asking the question in the room?

options.text: I assume someone more qualified already knows the answer
I ask freely and do not mind looking slow
I would rather look informed than become informed
I write the question down and never bring it

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Knowledge, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
quiz.scholar_reflection: The answer he got is one of the shortest and largest in the collection. It was waiting for whoever spoke first.

quiz.prompt: His poverty was the reason he had time to learn. Where has a limitation of yours turned out to be the opening?

options.text: I can name one clearly and I am grateful for it
I can see it in hindsight but never while it is happening
I am still waiting for mine to turn into anything
I suspect my limitations are just limitations

quiz.citation: Reflection on Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Knowledge, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
quiz.scholar_reflection: He did not romanticise the hunger. He described fainting and being trodden on. He simply also counted what it bought him.

quiz.prompt: He wept over his mother's refusal, then asked someone else to pray for her rather than arguing with her again. How do you carry a relative who will not hear you?

options.text: I keep arguing, and it keeps costing us both
I have gone quiet and I am not sure the silence is kindness
I pray for them and have stopped raising it directly
I have written them off and I do not like admitting it

quiz.citation: Sahih Muslim, Book of the Virtues of the Companions, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
quiz.scholar_reflection: He came back weeping the second time as well. Nothing about the outcome made the years of refusal retrospectively easy.

quiz.prompt: He said he was carrying two vessels and poured out only one, because the second would have got him stoned. When is holding something back the honest choice?

options.text: Almost never — I think withholding is usually cowardice
When the room cannot use it yet, whatever it costs me to sit on it
I withhold too easily and call it wisdom
I cannot tell my discretion from my fear

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Trials (Kitab al-Fitan), narrated by Abu Hurayrah
quiz.scholar_reflection: The man with the reputation for saying everything told the ummah, on the record, that there was something he was not saying.

quiz.prompt: He complained that he heard much and forgot it, and did something about it that same day. What is your actual relationship with what you have already been taught?

options.text: I collect far more than I retain and it does not trouble me
I keep little and I have stopped pretending otherwise
I hold a small amount very firmly
I only remember what I have had to use

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Knowledge — the spreading of Abu Hurayrah's cloak
quiz.scholar_reflection: He named the problem out loud to the one person who could fix it. Complaining about your memory to yourself is not the same act.
